tagline.text: A white sandbar shaped by the tide, and the Philippines' first marine reserve

children.text: A small coral island
15 minutes
by boat from the Oslob coast, and the site that became the Philippines' first marine protected area in
. Its white sandbar, which changes shape with the tides, and clear coral reefs are beautiful, making it a popular stop to pair with whale shark viewing in Oslob.
Sumilon Island is a small coral island about
1.5km

off the coast of Bancogon, Oslob, at the southeastern tip of Cebu Island. The whole island covers only a few dozen hectares, small enough to walk around in one loop, yet it's a place of great importance in the history of Philippine marine conservation. In

, researchers from Silliman University in Negros and local residents designated the waters around the island as a no-fishing zone, making it the Philippines' first Marine Protected Area, and it became the starting point of the community-based marine protected area model that later spread across the country.

What made Sumilon Island famous in photos is the white sandbar that forms at its northwest tip. The sandbar's shape and length change with the tides and seasons, and at low tide it creates the scene of a thin white path stretching out into the middle of the sea. The contrast of emerald and deep blue water on either side of the sandbar is striking, and on clear days you can see the mountain ranges of Cebu's main island and Negros Island across the water.

Much of the island is now operated by Bluewater Sumilon Island Resort. The island has an infinity pool facing the sea, a lagoon ringed by mangroves, and a trail crossing the island, making it good for a quiet retreat. Thanks to decades of protection, the surrounding waters have healthy coral and are also known as a snorkeling and diving spot.

It's most often visited as a half-day stop by travelers who came down at dawn to see the Oslob whale sharks, but many couples and family travelers also stay one or two nights at the resort to enjoy the whole island at leisure. It's recommended for travelers who want to rest on a quiet island for a day during a busy Cebu trip.

blocks.title: Walk the sandbar and take photos

children.text: Time your visit to low tide and the long, thin white sandbar reveals itself at its most beautiful. Shoot from the end of the sandbar looking back toward the island, and palm trees and the sandy path fit into one frame.

blocks.title: Snorkeling in the marine protected area

children.text: The coral reefs around the island are rich with coral and tropical fish thanks to long-term protection. Snorkel in the designated area, following the guide or resort's instructions.
A resort day pass lets you use the infinity pool that seems to merge with the sea. The view overlooking the sandbar and ocean is excellent.
In the lagoon on the island's interior, you can kayak or paddleboard for a close look at the mangrove forest. It stays relatively calm even on windy days.
Walking along the trail that crosses the island lets you see a cliff viewpoint and the shore on the opposite side. About
30 minutes–1 hour
is enough.
The coral walls and drop-offs around the island are among southern Cebu's leading dive sites. You can book a boat dive with a dive shop in Oslob.

Mactan-Cebu International Airport (CEB) is the closest, and it takes about
3 hours 30 minutes–4 hours 30 minutes
by car from the airport to Oslob. Going via Dumaguete Airport (DGT) in Negros, to Sibulan port, then by ferry to Liloan port (Santander), leaves only about
20–30 minutes
by car to Bancogon, which can shorten your travel time.
At Cebu City South Bus Terminal, take a Ceres bus on the 'Bato via Oslob' route or one bound for Santander, and get off at 'Bancogon (Sumilon jetty).' It takes about
3 hours 30 minutes–4 hours
, with air-conditioned bus fares around
. Choosing a whale shark day tour from Cebu City or Mactan that includes the Sumilon sandbar solves transport and the boat ride in one go.
From Bancogon jetty to Sumilon Island is about
15 minutes
by boat. Day pass holders and overnight guests use the resort boat, which usually runs round trips at set times from
until late afternoon. For a short sandbar-only visit, you charter a bangka, at around

per boat plus a separate environmental fee. Whether independent visits are allowed and the fees involved change often depending on resort and local government policy, so check the latest rules locally.
From
March
to
June
, when the sea is calm and sunlight strong, is when sandbar photos come out best. The dry season from December to
May
generally has little rain and is good for travel, but from
November to February

the northeast monsoon can bring higher waves to the island's east coast on some days. The sandbar's size varies greatly with the season and tide, and it can nearly disappear during periods of high waves.
During the rainy season, June–
November
, and typhoon season (mainly August–
November

), boat service can be suspended. The most important thing is the tide schedule. The sandbar is widest at low tide, so check a tide table before visiting and plan your schedule around the hours before and after low tide.

Bluewater Sumilon Island Resort is essentially the only accommodation on the island, with sea-view rooms and pool villas running about

a night. Staying on the island has the big advantage of letting you enjoy the sandbar quietly in the late afternoon and early morning, after the day visitors have left. To save on budget, it's recommended to stay at a guesthouse on the Oslob mainland coast (about
a night) and cross over as a day trip.

Meals on the island are taken at the resort restaurant, which serves Filipino seafood dishes and international cuisine. Day passes often include a food and drink credit. On the mainland at Bancogon and along the Oslob coastal road, there are simple restaurants selling grilled fish, kinilaw, and chicken barbecue, where you can get an inexpensive lunch.
Be sure to check the tide table. If you go at high tide, the sandbar is almost submerged and it's hard to see the scenery from photos.
For cleaning and maintenance, sandbar access is sometimes restricted on certain weekdays (such as Wednesdays), so check in advance.
You'll be asked to show ID when boarding the resort boat, so bring your passport or an ID card.
Day passes often sell out early on weekends and holidays, so it's best to book in advance.
There's no shade at all on the sandbar at midday. Prepare a hat, sunglasses, and a rash guard.
There may be rules on drone photography, so check whether it's permitted in advance.
Prepare plenty of cash on the mainland. There's no ATM around Bancogon jetty.
Inside the marine protected area, collecting or touching coral, shells, and marine life is prohibited.
At the tip of the sandbar, currents meet from both sides and can be fast, so don't swim out into deep water.
On days with high waves, boat service can be suspended, so don't insist on chartering a bangka.
Use reef-safe sunscreen, and always take your trash out with you.
Summer sun is very strong, and you can get sunburned even in a short time.
How to visit Sumilon and its fees change often depending on resort and local government policy. Check the latest notices before visiting.
